content: By the early 20th century, manufacturers began replacing the highly flammable cellulose nitrate film with cellulose acetate film as a safer alternative for motion picture and sheet film bases. This transition started with cellulose diacetate in 1909, followed by cellulose acetate propionate and cellulose acetate butyrate in the 1930s, and eventually cellulose triacetate and polyester bases in the late 1940s. These substitutes, collectively referred to as safety film, were less flammable than nitrate film. However, the motion picture industry continued using cellulose nitrate until cellulose triacetate met the stringent safety and performance standards of the industry in 1948. At the time, the poor chemical stability of cellulose acetate was not recognized, but it has since emerged as a significant threat to film collections. Decay 'Vinegar Syndrome' The first reported case of cellulose triacetate degradation occurred within a decade of its introduction in 1948. This report, submitted by the Government of India to the Eastman Kodak Company, described degradation in films stored in hot and humid climates. Similar reports followed from other regions with adverse environmental conditions. These observations prompted ongoing studies at Kodak laboratories starting in the early 1960s. By the 1980s, frequent reports of cellulose triacetate degradation, characterized by the release of acetic acid (vinegar), renewed focus on film stability. The Progression of Degradation In acetate film, acetyl (CH3CO) groups are attached to long cellulose molecular chains. When exposed to moisture, heat, or acids, these acetyl groups break away, releasing acetic acid. This acid diffuses to the surface of the plastic, producing a characteristic vinegar odor, which signals the onset of deterioration. The degradation process typically follows these stages: 1. Release of Acetic Acid: The initial stage of acetate base deterioration is marked by the release of acetic acid, leading to the vinegar smell. This is an early indicator of the progression of decay. 2. Embrittlement: In advanced stages, the plastic film base becomes brittle. The once-flexible and strong film weakens and can shatter under minimal tension. This brittleness results from the breakdown of the cellulose acetate polymer chains, which are shortened as acetic acid is released. The acidic environment accelerates the breaking of molecular bonds, further weakening the material. 3. Shrinkage: As the polymer chains break into smaller fragments and side groups detach, the plastic film begins to shrink. In severe cases, shrinkage can reach up to 10%, rendering motion picture film unusable with as little as a 1% reduction. The gelatin emulsion layer, which does not degrade as rapidly, often remains intact, leading to severe channeling in cut sheet films during later stages of degradation. 4. Crystalline Deposits and Bubbles: Advanced degradation can result in the appearance of crystalline deposits or liquid-filled bubbles on the emulsion. These are caused by plasticizers, additives in the plastic base, becoming incompatible with the film base and oozing to the surface. 5. Color Changes: In some cases, pink or blue hues appear in sheet films due to the reactivation of antihalation dyes in the gelatin layer. These dyes, which are intended to be colorless, revert to their original colors in the acidic environment created by the release of acetic acid. A-D Testing Strips The Image Permanence Institute developed A-D (acid-detection) indicator strips to monitor the extent of acid exposure in film collections. These strips change color from blue to green to yellow as acid levels increase. According to the User’s Guide, these tools are designed to assist in preserving photographic film collections, including sheet, roll, cinema, and microfilm. They help assess the damage to a film collection and guide steps to prolong its usability. Preservation and Storage Currently, there is no practical method to halt or reverse the degradation of cellulose acetate film. Research has explored various factors to slow the process, but temperature and humidity remain the most critical variables. According to the Image Permanence Institute, fresh acetate film stored at 65°F and 50% relative humidity can last approximately 50 years before vinegar syndrome begins. Lowering the temperature by 15°F while maintaining the same humidity can delay the onset by 150 years. Optimal storage conditions for cellulose acetate films involve a combination of low temperature and low relative humidity. During the early stages of decay, film content can be salvaged by transferring it to new film stock. However, once the film becomes brittle, it cannot be copied in its entirety. For sheet films, the gelatin emulsion, which often remains intact, can be separated from the shrunken base using solvents. The emulsion can then be photographed or transferred to a new support. This process is delicate, potentially hazardous due to the solvents used, and expensive for large collections. While degraded motion picture film cannot be restored this way, sheet films often can.
